How this lecture is built

Orientation: Three Cases, Five Objectives

Dr. Segal trained beginning in 1985, in the middle of the HIV epidemic, and the lecture is deliberately built from modified versions of his own patients. Every learning objective is delivered through one of three cases, so the fastest way to hold the material is to anchor each objective to its case.

🤒

Case 1 — Acute

27-year-old first-grade teacher with fever, sore throat, rash. Acute retroviral syndrome (primary HIV). HIV Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) ≈ 2,000,000 copies/mL.

Drives LO 1 (why treat early) and LO 2 (interpreting a test during the window period).

🩺

Case 2 — Chronic, Newly Diagnosed

32-year-old gay male notified of a positive test by the Maine CDC. CD4⁺ = 513 cells/µL, HIV RNA = 2,500 copies/mL.

Drives LO 2 (full testing algorithm), LO 3 (staging), and LO 5 (the whole management plan).

🫁

Case 3 — Advanced AIDS

38-year-old unhoused female, HIV diagnosed 13 years ago, out of care. CD4⁺ = 100 cells/µL, HIV RNA ≈ 1,525,000 copies/mL, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

Drives LO 3 (CD4⁺ thresholds), LO 4 (opportunistic infection vs. IRIS), LO 5 (prophylaxis).

Epidemiology and Law in Maine

  • 2012–2021: 30 new HIV diagnoses in Maine; 2.2 diagnoses per 100,000 people; majority male; age range 20–63 years, median 37 years.
  • HIV is a reportable disease in Maine. Through the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), the state has legal authority to quarantine, isolate, or mandate treatment for people living with a sexually transmitted infection — this includes syphilis and HIV.
  • Informed consent matters. Order HIV testing inside a shared decision-making conversation: explain that you are screening, what a positive result would mean, and what treatment would involve. Doing it this way produces markedly less patient distress.
🩺 Taking a Sexual History (Wiser, Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine 2024)

Use open-ended questions so you cast no aspersions and import no implicit bias:

  • Are you sexually active? Who are your partners? Do you have a current partner or partners?
  • How many partners in the past 6 months? Where do you typically meet partners?
  • What sexual activities do you participate in? — this is the question that determines whether you screen oral and anal sites, not just genital. Skipping it is how infections get missed.
  • Do your partners have a history of sexually transmitted infections? Do you have plans for pregnancy prevention? Any history of commercial sex work?

Brief History — Why the Naming Matters

YearEventWhy it is remembered
1959First recorded case — a Congolese man's blood sample was HIV positiveWhether he developed AIDS or died is unknown
June 5, 1981US CDC reports a rare pneumonia in young gay men in CaliforniaThe first AIDS alert
1981Second report: Kaposi sarcoma in gay men in New York and CaliforniaKaposi sarcoma is driven by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) in the immunosuppressed
1981–82Called "GRID" (Gay-Related Immune Deficiency), then "4H disease"4H = homosexuals, heroin users, hemophiliacs, Haitians — an epidemiology too narrow to be true
Late 1982Renamed AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome)Both older terms were still in casual use as late as 1985
1980sRyan White — a 13-year-old hemophiliac infected by transfusion, barred from school in IndianaForced the stigma into the courts and the public eye
⚠️ Stigma is Part of the Disease

Dr. Segal recounted a late-1980s home visit to a patient with advanced AIDS whose family had nailed him into a back room and cut a hole in the door to pass food through. Police, the fire department, and Adult Protective Services were needed to remove him. He offers it as the reason counseling, confidentiality, and the physician–patient relationship are not soft skills in HIV — they are the treatment.

LO 1 — Microbiology & Life Cycle → ART

Virology

HIV Basics: The Life Cycle Is the Drug Map

You cannot reason about antiretroviral pharmacology without the life cycle, because each drug class is named for the step it blocks. Learn the seven steps and the drug classes fall out of them for free.

🔑 Abbreviations Used in This Section
  • ART = Antiretroviral Therapy (in the 1990s this was called HAART — Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy).
  • RNA = Ribonucleic Acid, HIV's genetic material. DNA = Deoxyribonucleic Acid, the host cell's genetic material.
  • NRTI = Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor · NNRTI = Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor · INSTI = Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitor · PI = Protease Inhibitor.

The Seven Steps

  1. 1. Binding (Attachment) HIV attaches to receptors on the surface of a CD4⁺ cell — the CD4 receptor plus a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4). Blocked by: CCR5 antagonists (maraviroc), post-attachment inhibitors.
  2. 2. Fusion The viral envelope fuses with the CD4⁺ cell membrane, letting HIV enter. Blocked by: fusion inhibitors.
  3. 3. Reverse Transcription Inside the cell, reverse transcriptase converts single-stranded HIV RNA into double-stranded HIV DNA — this is what allows the virus to enter the nucleus and join host DNA. Blocked by: NRTIs and NNRTIs.
  4. 4. Integration In the nucleus, integrase inserts viral DNA into the cell's DNA. This is the irreversible step that creates the latent reservoir. Blocked by: INSTIs.
  5. 5. Replication The hijacked cell machinery makes long chains of HIV proteins.
  6. 6. Assembly New HIV proteins and RNA move to the cell surface and assemble into immature, non-infectious virus.
  7. 7. Budding Immature virus pushes out of the host cell and releases protease, which cleaves the long protein chains into the mature, infectious virus. Blocked by: protease inhibitors. Each infected cell produces hundreds of new variants.

Slide 38 — The HIV Life Cycle and the seven drug classes that stop it (HIVinfo.NIH.gov)

🧬 The Latent Reservoir — Why "Cure" Is the Wrong Word

After acquisition, HIV establishes a population of resting memory CD4⁺ T cells that carry integrated HIV DNA but are not actively producing virions — think of them as dormant. Current ART is designed to target actively replicating virus only. That is its functional limitation: the reservoir persists, capable of reactivating and spreading if treatment is interrupted.

This is exactly why cycling on and off therapy is so dangerous: it produces resistance mutations and viral rebound that can become untreatable. Suppression to undetectable levels lets people live full lives — but it is not a cure.

Rationale for Treating Acute HIV Infection

  • Preserves immune function and slows progression — slows the CD4⁺ decline and reduces HIV RNA levels.
  • Timing: ideally between 2 weeks and 6 months after seroconversion — or "same-day" therapy, started at the counseling visit.
  • Significantly reduces (does not eliminate) the latent reservoir — lower viremia, closer to a functional cure.
  • Suppresses plasma HIV RNA to undetectable levels.
  • Reduces transmission risk. For every 10-fold increase in viral load, transmission risk rises by a factor of 2.5.
  • Improves the inflammatory cytokine profile — HIV upregulates many inflammatory cascades.

Q: Why is early ART initiation recommended in HIV infection?

A. It prevents drug resistance  ·  B. It eliminates the latent reservoir  ·  C. It reduces viral set point and transmission risk  ·  D. It prevents IRIS  ·  E. It cures HIV and the development of AIDS

Answer — C

C. It reduces viral set point and transmission risk. This is the counseling point.

  • A — No: it reduces resistance with sustained adherence; breakthrough resistance still happens.
  • B — No: it significantly reduces the reservoir without eliminating it.
  • D — No: it reduces the risk of IRIS but does not prevent it.
  • E — No: there is no data suggesting ART leads to a cure.

First-Line Regimens (recognize, don't memorize)

Dr. Segal explicitly said he will not test the specific regimens — those belong to pharmacology and Dr. Vaughn's parallel lecture. Recognize the names, and know the two rules that always apply.

Biktarvy®

Bictegravir + tenofovir alafenamide + emtricitabine

The single-tablet regimen you see advertised on television; INSTI-anchored.

Dovato®

Dolutegravir + lamivudine

Two-drug INSTI regimen.

Descovy®

Tenofovir alafenamide + emtricitabine

Backbone paired with dolutegravir; TAF is the less nephrotoxic tenofovir.

Truvada®

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate + emtricitabine

Older tenofovir backbone; more proximal-tubule toxicity and bone loss.

Cabotegravir LA

Long-acting injectable INSTI

Also used for pre-exposure prophylaxis — prior use makes INSTI resistance testing important.

Boosters (not antiretrovirals)

Ritonavir · cobicistat

Added to inhibit cytochrome P450 3A4 and raise drug levels — the source of major interactions.

⚠️ Two Rules That Always Apply
  • If of childbearing potential, you must exclude pregnancy before starting — some regimens require a specific pregnancy protocol.
  • Adherence is the whole game. This is lifelong medication. Your job is to remove obstacles — prior authorizations, cost, side effects — not just to write the prescription.
LO 2 — CDC Testing Algorithm & Result Interpretation

Diagnosis

Testing: The Algorithm, the Window, and Acute Infection

🔑 Abbreviations Used in This Section
  • Ag/Ab = antigen/antibody · p24 Ag = the HIV-1 viral core protein antigen.
  • NAT = Nucleic Acid Test (the HIV-1 RNA test, also written RNA PCR — Polymerase Chain Reaction).
  • ARS = Acute Retroviral Syndrome (= primary HIV infection). EBV = Epstein–Barr Virus.
  • CDC = Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Case 1 — 27-year-old teacher

History: Seen in the emergency department for sore throat and fever, diagnosed "pharyngitis," discharged on clindamycin. Returns 3 days later worse — fatigue, fever, pharyngitis, myalgia. Blood cultures negative. Past history: class III obesity (BMI > 45), obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, anxiety. Social: no alcohol, nicotine, or cannabis; no pets or sick contacts. Reports living with a long-term girlfriend with a recent falling out and no recent sexual activity.

Exam: Tmax 101 °F, HR 108. Erythematous tonsils with white patches; prominent tender anterior and posterior cervical adenopathy; palpable, firm, tender spleen tip; pruritic erythematous papular rash on back, chest, arms; painful shallow oral ulcers.

Labs: White blood cells 2.5 with lymphocytosis; hemoglobin 11.0 with normal MCV (normocytic anemia); normal platelets; normal chemistries and liver function except low albumin, elevated total protein, and hypergammaglobulinemia.

Differential Diagnosis: Pharyngitis + Rash

CategoryEntityDiscriminating feature
BacterialGroup A StreptococcusCentor criteria (fever, tonsillar exudate, adenopathy, age, absence of cough); exudative tonsils; scarlet fever gives a "sandpaper" papular rash in young children, highly contagious
BacterialDiphtheriaRare; grayish-brown pseudomembrane
BacterialGonococcal (GC) pharyngitisSexual contact; look for migratory arthralgias (knee → wrist → shoulder → hip)
ViralCoxsackie AHerpangina or hand, foot and mouth disease
ViralAdenovirusPharyngoconjunctival fever; preauricular lymphadenopathy; outbreaks in schools, camps, military
ViralEBV mononucleosisProdrome, palatal petechiae, posterior cervical adenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytosis, papular eruption after ampicillin
ViralHerpes simplex virusGingivostomatitis — painful vesicles on oropharynx and lips
ViralAcute retroviral syndromeNON-exudative pharyngitis — this is the key discriminator from Group A strep
InflammatoryKawasaki diseaseChildren; oropharyngeal findings; coronary artery aneurysms (board favorite)
InflammatoryStevens–Johnson syndromeDrug-induced; mucosal involvement, full-thickness
InflammatoryBehçet diseaseOral–genital ulcerations plus papulopustules
InflammatoryDIHS/DRESSDrug reaction with eosinophilia; morbilliform rash
🩺 Two Pearls from the Case Discussion
  • Palatal petechiae occur in both Group A strep and mononucleosis — slightly more common in mono. In Group A strep, their presence increases the likelihood of an exudative presentation.
  • Hypergammaglobulinemia with a reversed albumin:globulin ratio was the historical tip-off for HIV when serology took 6 weeks to 3 months to return — especially alongside atypical lymphocytosis. It is still a useful clue.

TestResultInterpretation

Acute Retroviral Syndrome (Primary HIV)

  • After acquisition, more than 50% develop a transient, symptomatic illness — which then resolves on its own.
  • Clinical features are nonspecific and it is most often confused with mononucleosis.
  • Transmission risk is at its highest here — very high HIV RNA plus the person does not know their status.
  • Recognition at this stage decreases onward transmission through ART. "If you don't think about this condition, you are going to miss it."
  • Keep it on the differential for any teenager or 20-something with non-exudative pharyngitis + rash + splenomegaly + atypical lymphocytosis.

Slide 15 — Common (≥15%) and rare (<15%) manifestations of primary HIV infection. Fever 74.6%, fatigue 67.7%, myalgia 48.4%, skin rash 47.9%, headache 45.0%, pharyngitis 40.5% (Routy et al., Expert Rev Anti Infect Ther 2015)

Laboratory Markers Over Time — The Three Periods

Slide 16 — Temporal appearance of laboratory markers of HIV infection

PeriodApprox. timingWhat is detectable
Eclipse periodDay 0 – ~10 daysNothing. No diagnostic test can detect HIV in this interval
Acute infection~10 – 50 daysHIV RNA rises first, then p24 antigen appears and peaks (~day 30), then antibodies begin
Established (chronic) infection> ~50 days onwardHIV antibodies rise and persist; RNA settles at the viral set point; p24 falls away
🧬 Seroconversion = The Window Period

Seroconversion is the interval between acquiring HIV and the first detection of anti-HIV antibodies. How long that window is depends on the sensitivity of the assay used — which is why modern practice uses 4th- or 5th-generation assays that also detect p24 antigen, catching infection weeks before antibodies appear.

🔑 False Positives Are Rare

The false-positive rate for HIV testing with reflex is 0.22% (the slide value; Dr. Segal quoted it verbally as "less than 1%"). Practically: when a modern 4th/5th-generation assay with reflex is positive, the patient has HIV. Patients will sometimes not believe the result — these tests are very good.

The CDC HIV Testing Algorithm — Three Tiers

Slide 24 — Current CDC HIV testing algorithm

  1. Step 1 — HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay (with HIV-1 p24 antigen) Most laboratories (including NorDx and LabCorp) include the p24 antigen, which tests for acute HIV-1 infection. Non-reactive → stop (but if acute infection is suspected clinically, go straight to HIV-1 NAT, because of the eclipse period).
  2. Step 2 — HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay Performed as a reflex when step 1 is reactive. Determines which antibodies are present: HIV-1 alone, HIV-2, or "untypeable." If HIV antibodies are detected → manage as HIV infection: recommend ART initiation and provide counseling to prevent transmission.
  3. Step 3 — HIV-1 nucleic acid test (NAT / RNA PCR) Reflexed when the differentiation assay is negative or indeterminate. HIV RNA detected → positive for acute HIV-1 infection. RNA not detected → negative; provide or refer for prevention services including PrEP and PEP.
⚠️ "Why Not Just Do the NAT First?"

The nucleic acid test does detect HIV earlier than antibody or Ag/Ab tests. But it is roughly 3× the cost, far more complex for laboratories to run, and carries a real false-positive potential — particularly in low-risk individuals. That is why it sits at tier 3, not tier 1.

Q: A 32-year-old presents after notification of a positive HIV 4th-generation Ag/Ab test. According to current guidelines, what is the next test to perform after a reactive result?

A. HIV-1 Western blot  ·  B. HIV-1 RNA PCR (NAT)  ·  C. p24 antigen via ELISA  ·  D. Genotype resistance testing  ·  E. HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay

Answer — E

E. HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay — it tells you which form of HIV you are dealing with, or whether the strain is untypeable.

  • A — No: the Western blot detects antibodies only, has a longer detection window, inferior sensitivity, and cannot differentiate HIV-1 from HIV-2. It was the standard until 2014.
  • B — No: this is the third-tier confirmatory test, not the second.
  • C — No: p24 is already tested in combination with the Ag/Ab immunoassay; it detects acute HIV-1 infection.
  • D — No: genotype detects drug-resistance mutations and guides ART selection — it is not part of the diagnostic algorithm.

Baseline Laboratory Panel After a Confirmed Diagnosis

Case 2 — 32-year-old male, notified by Maine CDC

History: Identifies as a gay male (he/him); sexually active since 16 with multiple partners; frequent unprotected receptive anal intercourse, last 6 weeks ago. No prior sexually transmitted infections; two previous negative HIV tests, the last 2 years ago. Up to date on Tdap; no COVID-19 or hepatitis B vaccination. Review of systems: 5 lb weight loss per month, occasional diarrhea.

Exam: BP 110/56, HR 78, BMI 23. Acne vulgaris; seborrheic dermatitis of the glabella and nasolabial folds; no oral ulcers; submandibular, posterior cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy (non-tender, mass-like); otherwise unremarkable. The initial exam generally shows no HIV-specific findings unless acute retroviral syndrome or advanced disease is present.

🩺 Seborrheic Dermatitis Is a Screening Trigger

New-onset or unusually aggressive seborrheic dermatitis — classically at the glabella (between the eyebrows) and nasolabial folds — should make you think about HIV and screen for it.

⚠️ Toxoplasmosis Counseling (board favorite)

Tell patients with cats to have someone else handle the litter box — cat feces are a vehicle for Toxoplasma. Prophylaxis is generally added when the CD4⁺ count falls below 100 cells/µL.

🔑 Clinical Pearl — The Lymphocyte Shortcut

An absolute lymphocyte count < 1,000 cells/mm³ predicts a CD4⁺ count < 200 cells/mm³ (Annals of Emergency Medicine, September 1998). Useful because the complete blood count often returns before HIV-specific testing — it tells you immediately whether to start thinking about prophylaxis.

Genotype and Resistance Testing

  • Genotypic assays are preferred and recommended at entry into care, to guide selection of the initial regimen. Phenotypic assays cost far more and are reserved for HIV specialists.
  • They detect drug-resistance mutations in the relevant viral genes and require a plasma viral load of at least 500–1,000 copies/mL — so a well-suppressed patient may not be testable.
  • Fast turnaround (roughly 48–72 hours) and greater sensitivity for detecting mixtures of wild-type and resistant virus.
  • Covers NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, and INSTIs — but INSTI resistance often has to be ordered separately (a checkbox). Check it in anyone with prior long-acting cabotegravir exposure, whether for treatment or for PrEP.
  • Also used in virologic failure — people on ART with HIV RNA > 200 copies/mL.
LO 3 — CD4⁺ Count, Stage, and Opportunistic Infection Risk

Staging & Risk Stratification

CD4⁺ Count Tells You the Damage; Viral Load Tells You the Activity

🔑 The Single Most Testable Distinction in This Lecture
🛡️

CD4⁺ T-cell count

Degree of immune system impairment. Determines risk of opportunistic infections and who needs prophylaxis. It is the staging variable.

🦠

HIV RNA viral load

Active viral replication. Determines drug selection and monitors treatment response. It is the transmission variable (U = U).

Natural History — The Four F's

Slide 30 — Typical course of untreated HIV infection (HIV i-Base, 2016)

PhaseMnemonic "F"What is happeningApprox. duration
Acute infectionFlu-likeAcute retroviral syndrome; viral load peaks; CD4⁺ dips then partly recovers2–8 weeks, seroconversion at 1–3 months
Clinical latencyFeels "OK"Asymptomatic; slow CD4⁺ decline; viral set point established2–12 years
SymptomaticFalling countCD4⁺ drops, symptoms begin, viral load climbsVariable
Advanced / AIDSFinal crisisAIDS-defining opportunistic infections and malignancies2–3 years untreated
🩺 When to Start ART on This Curve

Start as early as possible — at the acute/latency stage — because that is where you preserve the immune reservoir, minimize the latent reservoir, and avoid the inflammatory cytokine damage. Waiting until the "falling count" phase means you are treating damage that is already done. CDC staging (2014) still runs stage 0 through stage 3, keyed on CD4⁺ count, with any AIDS-defining condition = stage 3. Dr. Segal said he will not test the specific stage boundaries, but will test specific CD4⁺ thresholds.

Physical Exam Findings Mapped to CD4⁺ Count

Erythematous candidiasis — CD4⁺ 200–500

Pseudomembranous candidiasis — CD4⁺ < 200

Oral hairy leukoplakia — CD4⁺ < 400

FindingAppearanceScrapes off?Typical CD4⁺
Erythematous candidiasisRed, flat patches on hard/soft palate—200–500 cells/µL
Pseudomembranous candidiasis (thrush)Dense white plaques forming a pseudomembraneYes — scrapes off with a tongue blade, may leave slight bleeding< 200 cells/µL
Oral hairy leukoplakiaPainless white, hairy/frond-like patches on the lateral tongue; driven by EBVNo — does not scrape off (the discriminator)< 400 cells/µL

Q: Which lab value best predicts risk of opportunistic infections in HIV?

A. HIV RNA viral load  ·  B. CD4⁺ T-cell count  ·  C. p24 antigen  ·  D. HIV genotype  ·  E. Absolute lymphocyte count

Answer — B

B. CD4⁺ T-cell count — the best measure of the degree of immune system impairment, and therefore of opportunistic infection risk and the need for prophylaxis.

  • A — No: viral load detects active replication and drives drug selection; undetectable = untransmittable (U = U).
  • C — No: p24 detects acute HIV-1 infection.
  • D — No: genotype detects drug-resistance mutations.
  • E — No: useful as a surrogate (< 1,000 cells/mm³ predicts CD4⁺ < 200), but not the best predictor.

🔑 CDC 2014 Stage 3 — The Definition of AIDS

Requires either:

  • CD4⁺ count < 200 cells/µL, OR
  • the presence of an opportunistic infection (an AIDS-defining condition).

Careful: community-acquired pneumonia by itself, without evidence of a compromised immune system, is not an opportunistic infection. In a patient with an impaired immune system, the same pneumonia does count as one. (Two or more episodes of bacterial pneumonia within 12 months is itself AIDS-defining.)

LO 4 — Opportunistic Infections vs. IRIS

Advanced Disease

Case 3: PJP, and the Trap of Getting Better Too Fast

🔑 Abbreviations Used in This Section
  • OI = Opportunistic Infection · IRIS = Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome.
  • PJP = Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (older name: PCP, Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia — you will see both on exams).
  • TMP/SMX = Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim®, Septra®) · LDH = Lactate Dehydrogenase.
  • A–a gradient = the alveolar-to-arterial oxygen difference · GGO = Ground-Glass Opacity on CT.
Case 3 — 38-year-old female, severe dyspnea × 3 weeks

History: HIV diagnosed 13 years ago, no consistent medical care; viral load and CD4⁺ unknown. Acquired heterosexually (frequent partners, unprotected intercourse); remains sexually active. Frequently unhoused, intermittent construction/temp work. Smokes 1–1.5 packs/day × 23 years; 3–4 beers nightly, more on weekends; daily cannabis (smoked); no injection drug use. Review of systems: 5–6 lb weight loss over 3 weeks, fevers, progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, chills, night sweats, malaise.

Exam: BP 90/56, HR 114, RR 22, T 100.5 °F, BMI 22. Unkempt, moderate distress, Fowler's position (sitting bolt upright), accessory muscle use, speaking only in short sentences. Seborrheic dermatitis; diffuse crackles throughout both lungs with no dullness to percussion; generalized lymphadenopathy; non-focal neurologic exam.

Risk Factors From the History That Shape the Differential

1

HIV, no prophylaxis

Opens the entire opportunistic-infection differential.

2

Unhoused

Markedly increased risk of tuberculosis.

3

Sexually active, unprotected, multiple partners

Ongoing sexually transmitted infection risk and onward transmission.

4

Heavy tobacco

Cerebrovascular damage; contributes to progression of neuro-AIDS.

5

Alcohol

Impairs judgment and engagement in care.

🩺 A Negative High-Resolution CT Argues Strongly Against PJP

The chest radiograph can be normal in up to 25% of PJP, but a normal high-resolution CT in someone with advanced HIV and a low CD4⁺ count makes PJP very unlikely. If you suspected it on a negative HRCT, you are most likely wrong.

Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PJP)

Why It Is an "Atypical" Fungus

  • Classified as a fungus based on RNA, cell wall, and key enzymes — but it does not grow in fungal culture.
  • Its cell wall contains cholesterol, not ergosterol — which is precisely why the standard antifungals that target ergosterol synthesis do not work, and why the treatment is TMP/SMX.
  • Cell wall is rich in β-1,3-D-glucan — the basis of the serum β-D-glucan test.
  • Main risk factor: immunosuppression of any cause — not just HIV (also kidney transplant, chemotherapy, chronic steroids).
  • Airborne transmission; exists in a latent state within alveolar macrophages.
DomainFindings
Symptoms (the triad)Fever (80–100%), non-productive cough (95%), progressive dyspnea (95%). 5–10% are asymptomatic
Physical examFever > 38.1 °C in > 80%; tachypnea 60%; crackles and rhonchi — but a normal chest exam in ~50%; frequent co-infection with thrush
CD4⁺ thresholdTypically < 200 cells/µL
Gas exchangePoor oxygenation with an increased A–a gradient
BiomarkersElevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH); elevated 1,3-β-D-glucan (> 80 pg/mL)
ImagingDiffuse interstitial or alveolar infiltrates, may be upper-lobe predominant; ground-glass opacities on CT; risk of pneumothorax

PJP Management

  1. Treat empirically when suspicion is high — CD4⁺ < 200 cells/µL, hypoxemia with an increased A–a gradient, and classic radiographic features. Do not wait for confirmation.
  2. TMP/SMX is the preferred regimen — oral for mild–moderate disease, intravenous for severe. Dose by weight based on the trimethoprim component.
  3. Add corticosteroids in moderate–severe disease — they reduce respiratory failure and mortality. Indications: worsening respiratory symptoms with PaO₂ < 70 mmHg or an A–a gradient ≥ 35 mmHg. Prednisone for 21 days (watch for candidiasis; consider thrush prophylaxis).
  4. Expect worsening for the first 2–3 days after starting treatment — killing the organism releases inflammatory material. This early worsening is not IRIS; it is too soon.
  5. Start ART within 2 weeks of beginning PJP treatment, to restore immune function.
  6. Prophylaxis: TMP/SMX if CD4⁺ < 200 cells/µL and not on ART, continued until the immune system reconstitutes.

Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS)

🧠 Definition

An exaggerated immune response to a variety of pathogens, occurring in response to ART-mediated recovery of the immune system. The immune system comes back online and overreacts to things that were sitting latent. It involves bacteria (Mycobacterium), viruses (HHV-8, CMV), fungi (Pneumocystis, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma), and autoimmune conditions. Mechanism: an adaptive antigen-specific T-cell response to the opportunistic infection plus dysregulation of the innate immune system.

📉

Paradoxical IRIS

The opportunistic infection is already known. You are treating it, you start ART, and symptoms worsen.

Example from lecture: a patient with PJP improves past the expected 2–3 day dip, then at 1–2 weeks develops worsening hypoxemia, worsening infiltrates on radiograph and CT, and requires intubation and mechanical ventilation.

🎭

Unmasking (ART-associated) IRIS

The opportunistic infection was undiagnosed until ART was started.

The patient has no known OI; you start ART; the recovering immune system produces inflammation that reveals the infection — often with worsening at the moment of diagnosis.

Comparison: Opportunistic Infection vs. IRIS

Clinical featureOpportunistic InfectionIRIS
Risk factorsLow CD4⁺ T-cell count; advanced HIV/AIDSAdvanced disease with low pre-treatment CD4⁺; a robust virologic and immunologic response; temporal association between ART start and symptom onset
CD4⁺ countLow — often < 100 cells/µLOften improving (but the pre-treatment CD4⁺ was low and the HIV RNA was high at diagnosis)
When it occursLate in the course of HIV, as CD4⁺ falls and AIDS developsIn the first few months after starting ART — median 48 days
PathophysiologyHIV-specific T- and B-cell responses with functional T-cell exhaustion plus ineffective T-cell regenerationMarked pro-inflammatory response to the pathogens causing OIs — "paradoxical or unmasking." The newly reconstituted immune system reacts too strongly
Associated diseasesPredominantly infectious — Cryptococcus, M. tuberculosis/MAC, PJP, JC virus, CMVImmune-mediated as well — sarcoidosis, autoimmune thyroid disease (Graves more than Hashimoto), Kaposi sarcoma, plus infectious causes
Relationship to ARTOccurs prior to ART initiationOccurs while or after ART initiation — in 10–20% of patients
Regimen dependence—The specific ART regimen chosen does not affect IRIS risk
⚠️ Case 3 Is a Textbook IRIS Set-Up

CD4⁺ 100 cells/µL, HIV RNA 1.5 million copies/mL, and an active opportunistic infection being treated — then ART started within 2 weeks. She has every risk factor. The answer is not to delay ART (delaying costs more than it saves); it is to anticipate IRIS, counsel the patient that worsening may occur, and keep it on your differential when she deteriorates on day 10 instead of improving.

Q: A patient with AIDS (CD4⁺ 90 cells/µL) is being treated for PJP with TMP/SMX and prednisone. ART is started on day 10. On day 21 she develops worsening hypoxemia and new pulmonary infiltrates. Her HIV RNA has dropped from 1.5 million to 12,000 copies/mL and her CD4⁺ has risen to 180 cells/µL. What is the most likely explanation?

Answer

Paradoxical IRIS. The tell-tale combination: a known, already-treated opportunistic infection, a short interval between OI treatment and ART start, and a robust virologic and immunologic response (falling viral load, rising CD4⁺) occurring alongside clinical worsening.

The improving laboratory numbers are the clue that separates this from treatment failure or a second infection — in true OI progression the virology would not be improving. Timing also fits: IRIS occurs within the first few months of ART, median 48 days. Note that the expected 2–3 day post-treatment worsening of PJP happens far earlier and is a different phenomenon.

LO 5 — Comprehensive, Patient-Centered Management Plan

Management

The Plan: Diagnose, Start ART, Prophylax, Vaccinate, Counsel

🔑 Abbreviations Used in This Section
  • PrEP = Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (before exposure) · PEP = Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (after exposure).
  • TDF = Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (older, more nephrotoxic) · TAF = Tenofovir Alafenamide (newer, less nephrotoxic) · FTC = Emtricitabine.
  • U = U = Undetectable equals Untransmittable · IAS-USA = International Antiviral Society–USA.

Step 1 — The Conversation (this is the intervention, not the preamble)

🗣️ Shared Decision-Making and Motivational Interviewing

Openers Dr. Segal uses: "What have you heard about HIV medicine?" · "What matters most to you?" · "What are your concerns about these medications?" — then identify barriers and build an approach to each one.

Insurers largely do not pay for this time, which is why clinicians skip it. In HIV you cannot skip it. If you cannot build a physician–patient relationship, everything downstream becomes much harder — and adherence is the whole disease.

Step 2 — Start ART (IAS-USA 2024 Recommendations, JAMA 2025)

  • Identify structural barriers that could delay the start of ART or impede engagement — housing, transport, cost, prior authorization, stigma.
  • Initiate ART as soon as possible — ideally within 7 days, and "same day" is acceptable and increasingly preferred.
  • Exclude pregnancy and screen all sexually active people with HIV for sexually transmitted infections.
⚠️ The Drug Interaction You Will Be Tested On

Boosters — ritonavir and cobicistat — are added to raise antiretroviral levels by inhibiting cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4).

Combine a booster with an over-the-counter nasal corticosteroid and the steroid accumulates → iatrogenic Cushing syndrome and adrenal suppression. Nasal steroids are sold over the counter, so if you do not warn the patient, no one will. The same CYP3A4 pathway governs several statins. Always ask about over-the-counter drugs, supplements, and herbal preparations at every visit — patients do not volunteer them.

Step 3 — Define the Goal: U = U

🎯 Sustained Virologic Response

Plasma HIV RNA below the level of detection: the CDC threshold is < 200 copies/mL, though some societies target 20–75 copies/mL. Undetectable = Untransmittable (U = U).

Why it matters:

  • Maintains the balance between CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ cells, protecting the immune system.
  • Reduces systemic inflammation.
  • Prevents the development of drug resistance by reducing mutation opportunity.
  • Improves quality of life and reduces morbidity and mortality.
🔑 The PARTNER Trial — the Evidence Behind U = U

Observed male–female and male–male couples (~3,000 individuals) across more than 74,000 condomless sex episodes. Zero HIV transmissions to HIV-negative partners while the partner with HIV maintained a durable undetectable viral load for ≥ 6 months.

Monitoring: check viral load every 3–4 months. Small temporary rises called "blips" occur and are not immediately alarming — follow the trend; as long as the curve stays essentially flat, there is no cause for concern.

Step 4 — Opportunistic Infection Prophylaxis by CD4⁺ Count

CD4⁺ thresholdProphylaxisTarget infection
< 200 cells/µLTMP/SMX (if not on ART; continue until immune reconstitution)Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
< 200 cells/µLCheck cryptococcal antigenCryptococcus (meningitis)
< 100 cells/µLProphylaxis in Toxoplasma IgG-positive patients (TMP/SMX covers both)Toxoplasmosis encephalitis
AnyTreat latent tuberculosis if PPD or interferon-gamma release assay is positiveTuberculosis

Step 5 — Immunizations

Slide 41 — Timing of vaccination in people with HIV (Dunlevy + Johnson, Topics in Antiviral Medicine 2024)

⚠️ The Live Vaccine Rule

The three live vaccines — varicella, yellow fever, and MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) — may be given only when the CD4⁺ count is ≥ 200 cells/µL. Two reasons: risk of vaccine-strain disease, and below that threshold the patient cannot mount an immunologic response, so you are simply wasting the dose.

Zoster: Zostavax® is the old live attenuated vaccine — contraindicated in immunocompromised patients and in HIV with CD4⁺ < 200. Shingrix® (recombinant, 2 doses) is the one to use in immunocompromised patients, including all transplant recipients.

VaccineCD4⁺ criteria
Mpox, Tdap, COVID-19, influenza, hepatitis AGive regardless of CD4⁺ count
Hepatitis BGive regardless of CD4⁺; in non-responders, revaccination can wait until CD4⁺ ≥ 200 with ART
PCV20 (pneumococcal conjugate)Give regardless of CD4⁺ (OI guidelines) or when CD4⁺ ≥ 200
PPSV23 (pneumococcal polysaccharide)Preferably defer until CD4⁺ > 200
Herpes zoster (recombinant)Give regardless of CD4⁺; responses are lower at low CD4⁺
Human papillomavirus (HPV)Responses are stronger with higher CD4⁺ and suppressed viral load
Varicella (live)Only when CD4⁺ ≥ 200
Yellow fever (live)Only when CD4⁺ ≥ 200
MMR (live)Only when CD4⁺ ≥ 200
Meningococcal conjugateBetter immunogenicity if CD4⁺ percentage > 15%, but deferral is not specifically recommended
RSVPresumably give regardless of CD4⁺ — not a live vaccine

Step 6 — Prevention: PrEP and PEP

Slide 43 — PrEP vs. PEP (HIVinfo.NIH.gov)

QuestionPrEP — Pre-Exposure ProphylaxisPEP — Post-Exposure Prophylaxis
When is it taken?Before HIV exposure — before sex, drug use, or other exposureAfter HIV exposure — started within 72 hours, taken for a month
Who is it for?People without HIV who are at risk of acquiring it from sex or from injection drug usePeople without HIV who may have been exposed: during sex, during a sexual assault, at work via needlestick or other injury, or by sharing injection equipment
How effective?Reduces sexual transmission by ~99% and injection-drug transmission by ~74%Prevents HIV when taken correctly but is not always effective — the risk falls to roughly < 1%. Start as soon as possible
Why the difference in effectiveness?Lower in people who inject drugs, thought to be because exposures are repeated and continuousSingle, defined exposure
🩺 Worked Example — Needlestick on Your Surgical Rotation

You are assisting, the surgeon loses focus and tags you with a needle. Notify the surgeon immediately, notify human resources, notify health services, get tested, and consider starting post-exposure prophylaxis while results are pending. Do not wait for the source patient's results before considering PEP — the 72-hour window is what matters.

Slide 45 — Algorithm prior to PrEP initiation (CDC clinical practice guideline, 2021 update)

⚠️ Three Pearls Before Starting PrEP
  • Always exclude pregnancy and consider a sexually transmitted infection screen.
  • If using TAF/FTC or TDF/FTC, check renal function and lipids. Both tenofovir formulations are toxic to the proximal tubule — worsening kidney function and Fanconi syndrome. TAF is the less nephrotoxic of the two, which is why it was developed. Both can also drive lipids up substantially.
  • Screen for hepatitis B. Emtricitabine and tenofovir both treat active hepatitis B — so if a patient with active hepatitis B stops them, hepatitis B can rebound.

Q: A 25-year-old female with multiple sexual partners is considering PrEP. Besides HIV testing, what additional evaluation is recommended prior to starting?

A. HLA-B*5701 genotype testing  ·  B. Tropism assay  ·  C. Bone density scan (DEXA)  ·  D. HIV genotype  ·  E. Baseline renal function + pregnancy testing

Answer — E

E. Baseline renal function and pregnancy testing — tenofovir affects kidney function, and pregnancy can be a contraindication to these medications.

  • A — No: HLA-B*5701 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity, and abacavir is not used in PrEP combinations.
  • B — No: a tropism assay determines which co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) the virus uses, establishing eligibility for a CCR5 antagonist (maraviroc).
  • C — No: a DEXA scan is useful to document baseline bone density, but it is not the required pre-PrEP evaluation.
  • D — No: HIV genotype detects drug-resistance mutations.

Levels of Prevention — How the Pieces Fit

🛡️

Primary

PrEP, PEP, condoms, HIV and sexually transmitted infection testing, risk-reduction counseling — stopping acquisition.

🔬

Secondary

Getting the HIV test — detecting disease early, before symptoms or transmission.

💊

Tertiary

Acting on a positive result — ART, prophylaxis, and reporting. HIV is reportable precisely because unmanaged transmission is a societal risk.

LO 5 (extended) — Long-Term Management

Chronic Disease

Chronic Complications: HIV as a Disease of Aging

Dr. Segal called this "probably one of the most important components of my talk." People with HIV now live close to normal lifespans, so the management plan has to extend past viral suppression into decades of cardiometabolic, bone, cognitive, and cancer risk.

🔥 "Inflammaging"

People aged ≥ 65 make up ~17–18% of the population (1 in 6), projected to rise to 22% by 2030; the prevalence of people with HIV over age 50 is projected to rise as well. Age-associated inflammation — "inflammaging" — is the major risk factor tying all the comorbidities together. It impacts both innate and adaptive immunity, increases cardiovascular disease, contributes to neurocognitive impairment, and accelerates functional limitation and frailty.

Dyslipidemia and Cardiovascular Disease

  • Occurs in up to 40% of individuals. Different regimens alter lipids differently: protease inhibitors (especially older ones) raise total cholesterol and triglycerides; INSTIs raise total cholesterol more than triglycerides.
  • HIV itself is a pro-atherogenic inflammatory state producing endothelial dysfunction. Markers include marked D-dimer elevation (indicating activation of both the coagulation and fibrinolytic systems) → atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction.
  • Standard cardiovascular risk tools underestimate risk in HIV. People with HIV present with coronary artery disease roughly 10 years earlier — a heart attack at 40 rather than 50.
  • Experts often adjust calculated risk upward by 1.5–2×; many guidelines target LDL cholesterol < 70 mg/dL.
  • Statin choice is an interaction problem. CYP3A4 interactions plus existing pill burden favor atorvastatin, low-dose rosuvastatin, and pitavastatin. Pitavastatin is often the better agent — it does not cause the statin-associated diabetes/metabolic effects seen with atorvastatin and rosuvastatin. Ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors are also used.

Fat Redistribution and Lipodystrophy

  • Changes in lean body mass and fat distribution occur in ~50%.
  • A marker of increased cardiovascular risk — patients gain epicardial and perivascular fat, which drives atherosclerosis directly.
  • Mechanism (a two-hit storm): HIV's effects on macrophages and T cells upregulate viral proteins within adipocytes, plus antiretroviral effects on adipocytes causing mitochondrial toxicity. Both subcutaneous and visceral white adipose tissue are involved.
  • Fat loss: facial lipoatrophy. Fat gain: dorsocervical lipomatosis ("buffalo hump"), abdominal lipohypertrophy.
  • Frequently complicated by insulin resistance, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) / steatohepatitis (MASH).
  • Management: insulin sensitizers (metformin, thiazolidinediones), GLP-1 / dual GLP-1-GIP agonists, injections, and surgery.

Diabetes and Insulin Resistance

  • New-onset diabetes occurs in about 14% of people with HIV.
  • Risk factors: coexisting hepatitis C (notably higher incidence — likely inflammatory), medications (atypical antipsychotics, steroids), low testosterone, ART-associated lipoatrophy and visceral fat accumulation, and HIV-related inflammation.
  • Protease inhibitors increase insulin resistance by downregulating the GLUT-4 transporter and reducing beta-cell insulin secretion. NRTIs contribute via mitochondrial toxicity.

Bone Loss and Low Bone Mineral Density

  • Multifactorial — HIV infection plus the effects of ART.
  • Increased osteoclastogenesis → increased osteolytic activity → accelerated bone density loss; plus deleterious effects on osteoblasts (less bone building).
  • TDF (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) → proximal tubule dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome) → hypophosphatemia, which accelerates the bone loss. This is why baseline DEXA is recommended with TDF.
  • Compounded by vitamin D deficiency and hypogonadism (especially in males) — the pathway to severe fractures.

Neurocognitive Dysfunction

  • HAND = HIV-Associated Neurocognitive Disorder, occurring in up to ~50%. Spectrum: asymptomatic → mild cognitive disorder → HAD (HIV-Associated Dementia).
  • Domains affected: attention, working memory, processing speed, executive function; leads to decline in instrumental activities of daily living.
  • Multifactorial: direct HIV damage; indirect factors (elevated cardiovascular risk, chronic alcohol/drug/tobacco use, long-term ART toxicity); persistent inflammation.
  • Neuroimaging: cortical and subcortical brain atrophy, abnormal white matter signal, variation in regional glucose metabolism.
  • ART is the mainstay, with attention to lifestyle and depression.

Malignancy Risk

🧬 Mechanisms and Cancers

Mechanisms: chronic antigen stimulation, inflammation, and cytokine dysregulation (Yarchoan + Uldrick, NEJM 2018).

Cancers: Kaposi sarcoma (the original AIDS-defining malignancy — driven by Human Herpesvirus 8 in the setting of immunosuppression), non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and anogenital cancers — anal, vulvar, and penile cancer. This is why baseline and serial cervical/anal Pap smears with high-risk HPV testing are in the panel.

Q: A 52-year-old man with well-controlled HIV (undetectable viral load, CD4⁺ 620 cells/µL) on an INSTI-based regimen has an LDL of 118 mg/dL and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 6% by the standard pooled cohort equation. How should you interpret and act on this?

Answer

The calculated risk is an underestimate. Standard cardiovascular risk tools underestimate risk in HIV, and people with HIV present with coronary artery disease about 10 years earlier than the general population. Experts adjust the calculated risk upward by 1.5–2× — putting this man closer to 9–12%.

Many guidelines target LDL < 70 mg/dL in HIV, so he warrants statin therapy. Choose with interactions in mind: pitavastatin, atorvastatin, or low-dose rosuvastatin — pitavastatin is favored for avoiding statin-associated diabetes. Remember his INSTI regimen also independently raises total cholesterol.

🎯 HIV — High-Yield One-Pager

By learning objective — LO1 life cycle · LO2 testing · LO3 CD4⁺ & staging · LO4 OI vs IRIS · LO5 management

LO 1 · LIFE CYCLE → ART

7 Steps and the Class That Blocks Each

  • 1 Binding: CCR5 antagonist (maraviroc), post-attachment inhibitor
  • 2 Fusion: fusion inhibitors
  • 3 Reverse transcription: NRTIs, NNRTIs
  • 4 Integration: INSTIs — creates the latent reservoir
  • 5 Replication · 6 Assembly (immature virus)
  • 7 Budding/maturation: protease inhibitors

Latent Reservoir

  • Resting memory CD4⁺ T cells with integrated HIV DNA, not producing virions
  • ART targets actively replicating virus only → no cure
  • Cycling on/off ART → resistance mutations + viral rebound

Why Treat Acute HIV Early

  • Preserves immune function, slows CD4⁺ decline
  • Reduces viral set point + transmission risk (the exam answer)
  • Reduces — not eliminates — the reservoir; does not prevent IRIS; not a cure
  • 10× ↑ viral load → transmission ↑ 2.5×
  • Start 2 wks–6 mo post-seroconversion, or same day

Always Applies

  • Exclude pregnancy if childbearing potential
  • Adherence = the whole disease
  • Boosters (ritonavir, cobicistat) inhibit CYP3A4
LO 2 · CDC TESTING

Three-Tier Algorithm

  • 1. HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab immunoassay with p24 Ag. Non-reactive → stop (unless acute suspected → go to NAT)
  • 2. Reactive → HIV-1/HIV-2 Ab differentiation immunoassay (the "next test" answer)
  • 3. Negative/indeterminate → HIV-1 NAT (RNA PCR). RNA detected = acute HIV-1
  • NAT is not tier 1: 3× cost, complex, false positives in low-risk
  • Western blot obsolete since 2014 — Ab only, can't separate HIV-1/2
  • False-positive rate with reflex = 0.22%

Three Time Periods

  • Eclipse (0–10 d): nothing detectable
  • Acute (10–50 d): RNA first → p24 Ag (peaks ~d30) → Ab begins
  • Chronic (>50 d): antibodies; RNA at set point
  • Seroconversion = window between acquisition and first Ab detection

Acute Retroviral Syndrome

  • >50% get a transient symptomatic illness that self-resolves
  • Fever 74.6%, fatigue 67.7%, myalgia 48.4%, rash 47.9%, pharyngitis 40.5%
  • NON-exudative pharyngitis vs exudative Group A strep
  • Mimics mono: splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytosis, posterior cervical nodes; Monospot negative
  • Hypergammaglobulinemia + reversed albumin:globulin = classic tip-off
  • Highest transmission risk (huge RNA + unaware)

Baseline Panel — Special Tests

  • Genotype at entry into care (resistance 5–15%); needs VL ≥500–1,000; INSTI often a separate checkbox
  • HLA-B*5701 → abacavir hypersensitivity
  • Tropism → CCR5 vs CXCR4 (maraviroc eligibility)
  • G6PD → hemolysis risk
  • CMV IgG neg → needs CMV-negative blood if transfused
  • HBsAb non-reactive → give full hepatitis B series
LO 3 · CD4⁺ & STAGING

The Core Distinction

  • CD4⁺ count = immune impairment → OI risk + prophylaxis (best predictor)
  • Viral load = active replication → drug selection + U=U
  • Pearl: absolute lymphocytes <1,000/mm³ predicts CD4⁺ <200

Four F's (natural history)

  • Flu-like (acute, 2–8 wk) → Feels OK (latency, 2–12 yr) → Falling count (symptomatic) → Final crisis (AIDS, 2–3 yr)

AIDS = CDC 2014 Stage 3

  • CD4⁺ <200 cells/µL OR an opportunistic infection
  • CAP alone without immune compromise ≠ an OI; ≥2 episodes in 12 mo is AIDS-defining

OIs by CD4⁺

  • 200–500: tuberculosis
  • <200: PJP, Cryptosporidium, candida, fungal pneumonia
  • <100: toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing lesions), candida/HSV/CMV esophagitis
  • <50: CMV, Cryptococcus (India ink), MAC, primary CNS lymphoma (EBV)

Oral Findings

  • Erythematous candidiasis: CD4⁺ 200–500
  • Pseudomembranous thrush: CD4⁺ <200 — scrapes off
  • Oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV, lateral tongue): CD4⁺ <400 — does NOT scrape off
LO 4 · OI vs IRIS

PJP Essentials

  • Atypical fungus: cholesterol, not ergosterol cell wall; doesn't grow in fungal culture; rich in β-D-glucan
  • Triad: fever (80–100%), dry cough (95%), progressive dyspnea (95%)
  • Normal chest exam in ~50%; CXR normal in up to 25%; CT = GGOs with peripheral sparing
  • Labs: CD4⁺ <200, ↑ A–a gradient, ↑ LDH, β-D-glucan >80 pg/mL
  • Tx: TMP/SMX (dose by trimethoprim component), PO mild–mod / IV severe
  • Steroids if PaO₂ <70 or A–a ≥35 → prednisone × 21 d
  • Worsens 2–3 d after starting Tx (expected, not IRIS)
  • Start ART within 2 weeks; prophylax with TMP/SMX if CD4⁺ <200 and not on ART

IRIS — Two Forms

  • Paradoxical: known OI, being treated, worsens after ART start
  • Unmasking: OI undiagnosed until ART started, then revealed

OI vs IRIS Discriminators

  • Timing: OI = late/before ART · IRIS = first few months of ART, median 48 days
  • CD4⁺: OI = low (<100) · IRIS = improving (low pre-treatment)
  • Mechanism: OI = T-cell exhaustion · IRIS = marked pro-inflammatory overreaction
  • Diseases: OI = infectious · IRIS = also immune-mediated (sarcoidosis, Graves, Kaposi)
  • Occurs in 10–20%; regimen choice does not change risk
LO 5 · MANAGEMENT

Start ART (IAS-USA 2024)

  • Identify structural barriers first
  • ART ASAP — ideally ≤7 days, same-day acceptable
  • Exclude pregnancy; screen all sexually active patients for STIs

Goal: U = U

  • CDC threshold <200 copies/mL (some societies 20–75)
  • PARTNER trial: ~3,000 people, >74,000 condomless episodes, zero transmissions with durable suppression ≥6 mo
  • Monitor VL every 3–4 months; transient "blips" are OK if the trend is flat

Prophylaxis Thresholds

  • CD4⁺ <200: TMP/SMX for PJP; check cryptococcal antigen
  • CD4⁺ <100: toxoplasmosis prophylaxis if IgG+ (TMP/SMX covers both)
  • Counsel: someone else handles the cat litter

Vaccines

  • Live vaccines — varicella, yellow fever, MMR — only if CD4⁺ ≥200
  • Zostavax® = live, avoid; Shingrix® (recombinant, 2 doses) for immunocompromised
  • Tdap, influenza, COVID-19, hepatitis A/B, mpox: regardless of CD4⁺
  • PPSV23: preferably defer until CD4⁺ >200

PrEP vs PEP

  • PrEP = before exposure; ~99% ↓ sexual, ~74% ↓ injection drug use
  • PEP = after exposure; start within 72 h, take × 1 month
  • Pre-PrEP: renal function + pregnancy test (the exam answer), STI screen, hepatitis B screen
  • Tenofovir → proximal tubule → Fanconi; TAF less nephrotoxic than TDF
  • FTC + tenofovir treat hepatitis B → stopping causes rebound

Chronic Complications

  • "Inflammaging" ties them all together
  • Dyslipidemia ~40%; CAD 10 yr earlier; adjust risk 1.5–2×; LDL target <70; prefer pitavastatin
  • Lipodystrophy ~50%; diabetes ~14% (PIs ↓ GLUT-4)
  • Bone loss: TDF → Fanconi → hypophosphatemia; DEXA
  • HAND up to 50%; ART is the mainstay
  • Malignancy: Kaposi (HHV-8), non-Hodgkin lymphoma, anal/vulvar/penile
